rows.title: Waymo will recall software after its self-driving cars passed stopped school buses
rows.standfirst: Waymo is issuing a software recall for its self-driving cars after reports the company's autonomous vehicles failed to stop for school buses.

rows.title: 7 deaths and hundreds of injuries are linked to faulty Abbott glucose monitors
rows.standfirst: About 3 million glucose monitoring sensors were potentially affected by a production error that caused incorrect low glucose readings.

rows.title: How hurricanes became a hot investment
rows.standfirst: A few years ago, the Jamaican government started making an unusual financial bet. It went to investors around the world asking if they'd like to wager on the chances a major hurricane would hit the island in the next couple of years.

rows.title: Appeals court hands Trump a victory, OK'ing firings of two independent agency heads
rows.standfirst: The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled 2 to 1 that President Trump's firings of Democratic members of the Merit Systems Protection Board and the National Labor Relations Board were lawful.

rows.title: EU hits Elon Musk's X with $140 million fine over business practices
rows.standfirst: The fines were due to the platform's misleading use of blue check marks to identify verified users and a lack of transparency over ads and data access for researchers.

rows.title: Netflix will buy Warner Bros' studio and streaming businesses for $72 billion
rows.standfirst: The merger, announced Friday, would bring two of the industry's biggest players in film and TV under one roof. Beyond its television and motion picture division, Warner owns HBO Max and DC Studios.

rows.title: NPR battles Trump executive order in court
rows.standfirst: NPR was in court for a pivotal hearing arguing that the Trump administration had broken the law with its treatment of public media.

rows.title: Chips up, rent down, and are people really skimping on holiday gifts?
rows.standfirst: It’s … Indicators of the Week! Our weekly look at some of the most fascinating economic numbers from the news. On today’s episode: A big goshDRAM memory problem, a holiday spending mystery, and apartment rental prices … decline?! Related episodes:

rows.title: 'New York Times' lawsuit creates a new headache for Pentagon chief Hegseth
rows.standfirst: The Times accuses Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth of violating its constitutional rights with a press policy that, the paper says, deprives the public of access to critical national security information.

rows.title: In an era of rising prices, computers have gotten cheaper. (And why that may end)
rows.standfirst: One thing has bucked the trend of rising prices: computing. Technological advances have underpinned a consistent drop in the cost of computers. But experts say that this may be reaching a limit.

rows.title: U.S. health care is broken. Here are 3 ways it's getting worse
rows.standfirst: One year after UnitedHealthcare's CEO was shot and killed, the crisis in U.S. health care is intensifying — even for the companies and investors who make money from it.

rows.title: A little doomsday feeling is weighing on the economy
rows.standfirst: It is a special edition of the Beigies Awards where one regional Federal Reserve Bank will receive lifetime achievement recognition. Today on the show, we speak to its President about the value of economic anecdotes. Related episodes:

rows.title: Trump administration rolls back fuel economy standards
rows.standfirst: At the White House this afternoon, President Trump said he was terminating "ridiculously burdensome" fuel economy rules. It's part of a series of changes relaxing or eliminating rules promoting cleaner cars.

rows.title: Check your cheese: Shredded and grated varieties are recalled nationwide
rows.standfirst: The FDA is urging customers to toss certain brands of grated Pecorino Romano; at the same time, it escalated an existing recall of numerous shredded cheeses.

rows.title: Is AI slopifying the job market? (Two Indicators)
rows.standfirst: Vote for us in NPR’s People’s Choice Awards: npr.org/peopleschoice

rows.title: Questions of accuracy arise as Washington Post uses AI to create personalized podcasts
rows.standfirst: The Post calls the podcast an "AI-powered tool" that turns its articles into an audio news digest.

rows.title: Should you use buy now, pay later? Experts share 4 tips to know
rows.standfirst: The payment option is booming among online holiday shoppers this year. But like any form of credit, it comes with drawbacks. Here's how to use BNPL responsibly — and protect yourself from risk.

rows.title: When Chicago pawned its parking meters
rows.standfirst: In 2008, Chicago’s budget was in a bad place. The city needed money. One way to raise money was to increase property taxes, but what politician wants to do that? So instead, Mayor Richard M. Daley’s administration looked around at the resources the city had, and thought, ‘Any of this worth anything?’ They opted to lease out the city’s metered parking system — to privatize all 36,000 of its parking meters.

rows.title: CNN has endured turmoil for years. Now Trump wants role in its fate
rows.standfirst: In the corporate battle over parent company Warner Bros. Discovery, CNN's fate remains up for grabs. President Trump wants a say in what happens next.

rows.title: Nvidia chips for China, frozen Russian funds, and a lot of self-checkout stealing
rows.standfirst: It’s … Indicators of the Week! Our weekly look at some of the most fascinating economic numbers from the news.

rows.title: Reddit challenges Australia's world-first law banning children under 16 from social media
rows.standfirst: Global online forum Reddit files a court challenge to Australian law blocking children under 16 from holding accounts on the world's most popular social media platforms.

rows.title: Farmers welcome Trump's $12 billion aid package, say additional relief is needed
rows.standfirst: President Trump says he's sending $12 billion in aid to American farmers who are reeling from global trade disruptions. Those include inflation and Trump's tariffs that are making fertilizer and farm equipment more expensive, and the President's trade war with China which closed a huge market for American soybean exports.

rows.title: Elizabeth Warren says both bids to buy Warner Bros. Discovery are bad for consumers
rows.standfirst: Sen. Elizabeth Warren cautions that the sale of Warner Bros. Discovery to either Netflix or Paramount Skydance could reduce competition and concentrate power over what films and news American see.

rows.title: Trump calls affordability crisis a 'hoax.' The data tells a different story
rows.standfirst: As Democrats campaigning on affordability pick up wins, Trump's messaging about a strong economy is at odds with widespread voter sentiment that he's not doing enough to tackle rising costs.

rows.title: How to make $35 trillion ... disappear
rows.standfirst: You may be familiar with the AI-fueled stock market boom. Well, former International Monetary Fund Chief Economist Gita Gopinath warns it could mirror the dot-com boom of the late 1990s. But worse. She calculates a similar crash could erase $35 trillion in global wealth. Today on the show, what would that mean for the US and global economies?

rows.title: The Fed is expected to cut rates. And, Afghan CIA fighters feel abandoned by the U.S.
rows.standfirst: The divided Federal Reserve is considering cutting interest rates today. And, Afghans in the U.S. who fought for the CIA say they feel abandoned by the agency.

rows.title: Brett Cooper says she makes up her own mind — about Trump and everything else
rows.standfirst: NPR's Steve Inskeep asks conservative commentator Brett Cooper about her YouTube following, her recent criticisms of President Trump and her opinion of Nick Fuentes.

rows.title: Feeling burned out? There's a word for that in Mandarin Chinese
rows.standfirst: How an obscure term used in anthropology leaped from the pages of academia into the Chinese meme world and then became part of Chinese government policymaking.

rows.title: A divided Federal Reserve cuts interest rates for a 3rd straight time
rows.standfirst: The Fed lowered its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point, in an effort to shore up a weakening job market. With inflation remaining stubbornly high, it was not a slam dunk decision.

rows.title: Bitcoin miners are betting on AI over crypto
rows.standfirst: If you want to make Bitcoin, you need powerful computers and a lot of energy. Well, it turns out the same infrastructure needed for Bitcoin mining is pretty valuable in the era of AI. Today on the show, why some miners are starting to throw in the towel on crypto in favor of supporting AI infrastructure. Related episodes:

rows.title: Lawmakers threaten Attorney General Bondi with contempt over incomplete Epstein files
rows.standfirst: The Justice Department is defending its initial release of documents related to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, saying lawyers are still going through them to ensure victims are protected.

rows.title: A radio station in Amsterdam is a lifeline for Sudan. After USAID cuts, it's faltering
rows.standfirst: Budget cuts threaten the future of Amsterdam-based Radio Dabanga, which has served as an information lifeline for Sudanese people about their war-torn country.

rows.title: Apple, Google tell workers on visas to avoid leaving the U.S. amid Trump immigration crackdown
rows.standfirst: With months-long consulate and embassy delays being reported, the two tech companies say staying put in the U.S. right now could prevent workers from getting stranded in their home countries.

rows.title: What AI data centers are doing to your electric bill
rows.standfirst: As a country, we are spending more to get data centers up and running than we spent to build the entire interstate highway system. (Yes, that’s inflation-adjusted.) With tech companies spending hundreds of billions of dollars on AI, data centers have kind of become the thing in the US economy.

rows.title: 4 common scams to watch out for this holiday season
rows.standfirst: Don't get swindled while buying those last-minute gifts. Amy Nofziger, a fraud specialist with AARP, shares top schemes she's been seeing this season — and tips on how to protect yourself.

rows.title: Meet the new WaPo food critic who won't dine in anonymity
rows.standfirst: NPR's Leila Fadel tags along for lunch with Elazar Sontag, the Washington Post' s new food critic.

rows.title: In the shadow of U.S. export controls, China rallies its own chip industry
rows.standfirst: The chip industry in China is hustling to overcome a Western tech choke hold, even as President Trump appears poised to loosen U.S. chip restrictions.

rows.title: Tariffs. Consumer sentiment. Cape Ratio. Pick The Indicator of The Year!
rows.standfirst: 2025 was a wild year for the U.S. economy. Tariffs transformed the global economy, consumer sentiment hit near-historic lows, and the stock market hit scary, spooky, blood-curdling new heights! So … which of these economic stories defined the year?

rows.title: Inflation cools slightly in November as worries about affordability grip Americans
rows.standfirst: The cost of living in November was up 2.7% from a year ago, according to a report Thursday from the Labor Department. That's a smaller annual increase than for the 12 months ending in September.

rows.title: Under Trump, 317,000 workers are out of the government. Here are 3 of their stories
rows.standfirst: Mass firings, buyouts and heightened uncertainty led to an exodus of federal workers in 2025. More than 300,000 employees will be out of the government by the end of December.

rows.title: Lone FCC Democrat warns of political pressure on media if agency loses independence
rows.standfirst: The only Democrat on the Federal Communications Commission says chairman Brendan Carr's belief that the FCC isn't independent leaves news media vulnerable to political pressure.

rows.title: Catching up with a fired federal worker, a shrimper and a fraudster
rows.standfirst: After a firehose of economic news in 2025, we wanted to check back on some of the people we’ve heard from on our show. Today, we check in with a former federal employee caught in the Trump administration's wood chipper, a Louisiana shrimper on Trump’s tariffs and an update on a financial aid scam.

rows.title: Pulitzer Prize-winning correspondent Peter Arnett has died
rows.standfirst: Peter Arnett, the Pulitzer Prize-winning reporter who spent decades dodging bullets and bombs to bring the world eyewitness accounts of war from Vietnam to Iraq, has died. He was 91.

rows.title: PM does a pop culture draft: 1999 edition
rows.standfirst: Welcome to the inaugural Planet Money Pop Culture Draft! In today's episode (a Planet Money+ episode we’re releasing into the main feed) we're gonna go back to the year 1999. Three hosts, Kenny Malone, Wailin Wong, and Jeff Guo, go head to head and each drafts a “team” of economic pop culture. So a movie, a song, and a wild card pick that best represents the Planet Money spirit!

rows.title: Trump's BBC lawsuit: A botched report, BritBox, and porn
rows.standfirst: President Trump's lawsuit alleges that the BBC's fall 2024 documentary was "a brazen attempt" to harm his re-election. The BBC has apologized but rejects his claim.

rows.title: What to know about Nick Shirley, the YouTuber alleging day care fraud in Minnesota
rows.standfirst: Shirley is a 23-year-old self-described "independent YouTube journalist" who made prank videos in high school before pivoting to politics. He participated in a White House roundtable in October.

rows.title: Indicators of the Year, Past and Future
rows.standfirst: 2025 is finally over. It was a wild year for the U.S. economy. Tariffs transformed global trading, consumer sentiment hit near-historic lows, and stocks hit dramatic new heights! So … which of these economic stories defined the year?

rows.title: Why Americans don't want to move for jobs anymore (Encore)
rows.standfirst: Americans are moving at record lows for work. What’s driving people to, well, not drive cross-country for jobs? On today’s episode, we explore the rising homebody economy.

rows.title: Judge orders Trump administration to continue to seek funding for the CFPB
rows.standfirst: The order is the latest in a complex legal battle over the fate of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, a watchdog agency.

rows.title: Gilded Age 2.0? (Encore)
rows.standfirst: To hear President Trump tell it, the late 1800s, i.e. the Gilded Age, were a period of unparalleled wealth and prosperity in the U.S. But this era was also marked by corruption and wealth inequality. Sound familiar? On today's show, is history repeating itself?

rows.title: FIFA president defends World Cup ticket prices, saying demand is hitting records
rows.standfirst: The FIFA President addressed outrage over ticket prices for the World Cup by pointing to record demand and reiterating that most of the proceeds will help support soccer around the world.

rows.title: Electric vehicles had a bumpy road in 2025 — and one pleasant surprise
rows.standfirst: A suite of pro-EV federal policies have been reversed. Well-known vehicles have been discontinued. Sales plummeted. But interest is holding steady.

rows.title: The cautionary tale of a recovering day trading addict (Encore)
rows.standfirst: Seasons greetings from the The Indicator! On today's show, the story of a man who started buying and selling stocks as a hobby — and got seriously addicted. We also speak with a neuroeconomist about the human brain on day trading.

rows.title: Memory loss: As AI gobbles up chips, prices for devices may rise
rows.standfirst: Demand for memory chips currently exceeds supply and there's little chance of that changing anytime soon. More chips for AI means fewer available for other products such as computers and phones. That could drive up those prices too.

rows.title: Marijuana rescheduling would bring some immediate changes, but others will take time
rows.standfirst: President Trump set the process in motion to ease federal restrictions on marijuana. But his order doesn't automatically revoke laws targeting marijuana, which remains illegal to transport over state lines.

rows.title: Clean energy is surging despite political attacks. But a slowdown may be looming
rows.standfirst: The U.S. is forecast to add a lot less power from renewables than analysts previously expected. The potential slowdown comes as electricity demand is rising faster than it has in decades.

rows.title: The Rest of the Story, 2025
rows.standfirst: Most stories keep going even after we set down our microphones and the music fades up. That's why, at the end of each year, we look back and we take stock.

rows.title: The secret to Nintendo's success (Encore)
rows.standfirst: For the next week, we're running some of our favorite shows from this year. On today's show, a brief history of Nintendo and how a small playing card company in Japan became a gaming juggernaut. This piece originally aired June 16, 2025. Related episodes:

rows.title: Jimmy Kimmel jokes about fascism in an 'alternative Christmas message' for Britain
rows.standfirst: In an "alternative" message to the king's annual Christmas speech, Kimmel told British viewers that "from a fascism perspective, this has been a really great year," for the United States.

rows.title: The summer I turned binge-y
rows.standfirst: On the eve of Netflix shoveling a fourish-hour chunk of Stranger Things onto Christmas Day, we visit the past, present, and future of binge-dropped television shows.

frame: Up to15 visible Business-archive cards at four fixed weekly endpoints, restricted to each block; not a full-publication census
